chapters.title: Belief in Oneness of Allah (Attributes of Allah and the Requisite of Tawheed)

questions.question: Explain the belief in Tawheed.
questions.answer: Belief in Tawheed (faith in the Oneness of Allah) is the first and most fundamental article of faith in Islam. The word "Tawheed" literally means to affirm oneness, while "Aqeedah" (derived from "Aqd", to tie fast) refers to the thoughts and ideas a person firmly believes in and which shape his character and attitudes. In Islamic terminology, Aqeedah-e-Tawheed means that the Creator, Owner and Sovereign of this universe is Allah Almighty alone, Who is from eternity and will last forever, with neither beginning nor end. He is the only God; He has created everything with perfect proportion and order. His knowledge encompasses every particle of the universe, He sees all, hears all, gives provisions, and guides. There is no precedent or example for Him; He is the owner of the gain and loss of creatures and the Giver of eternal life after death; He has no partner. To believe in this with firm conviction of the heart and to express it by the tongue when necessary is called Tawheed. It is the essence of all worship and the starting point of the call of every Prophet from Hazrat Adam to Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH), and the first part of the Kalima Tayyibah, "La ilaha illa Allah", reflects this very belief.
questions.explanation: From the lesson's definitions of Aqeedah and Tawheed on page 65 (image 68); the belief is the first cardinal article of faith and the foundation of religion commanded by Allah and all the Prophets.

questions.question: Write a detailed note on the requisite of Tawheed.
questions.answer: The requisites (essential requirements) of Tawheed are those basic beliefs and practices without which the claim of believing in Allah Almighty becomes meaningless. First, Allah Almighty is unique and incomparable: "There is nothing like Him" (Surah Al-Shura: 11), so He must be believed in as an incomparable being. Second, there is only Allah Almighty whose pleasure man should seek. Third, all acts that fall into the category of worship must be reserved for Allah alone: prostration, vows and prayers should be kept for Him, supplications should be made to Him, refuge should be sought from Him, and only He should be called for help, as Allah says "Do not worship anyone other than Him" (Surah Al-Isra: 23). Fourth, all emotions and feelings in which the spirit of worship lies—praise and gratitude, hope and trust, fear and piety, true love and devotion, humility and submission—should be reserved for Allah Almighty alone. Fifth, the only sovereign of the whole universe is Allah; He alone has the right to command and forbid, He is the real Legislator, and He alone has the right to set the law of life, to forgive or to punish. Sixth, we should live this worldly life according to the guidance and commands sent by Allah Almighty, believing in Him with all His attributes. These requirements are so crucial that denying any of them makes the claim of believing in Allah meaningless; no one can be a true Muslim unless he believes in Tawheed with its full meaning.
questions.explanation: Drawn from the "Requirements of Tawheed" section (pages 68-69, images 71-72), which lists uniqueness of Allah, exclusive worship, exclusive worship-emotions, exclusive sovereignty, and living by Allah's guidance.

questions.question: What is the concept of faith (Iman)?
questions.answer: Faith (Iman) rests on firm conviction of the heart. The word "Aqeedah" is derived from the Arabic "Aqd", meaning to tie fast, and refers to the thoughts and ideas a person firmly believes in, which affect his character and attitudes. Belief in Tawheed is the first cardinal article of faith in Islam, and a Muslim must first reform his belief before all else.
questions.explanation: Based on the definition of Aqeedah and belief on page 65 (image 68).

questions.question: What is meant by worship?
questions.answer: Worship (Iba'dat) is to live according to the blessed life of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) with the intention of gaining the pleasure of Allah Almighty. It includes every action that Allah has commanded to do and abstaining from whatever He has forbidden, and it is the practical form of man's direct contact and relationship with Allah.
questions.explanation: Based on the lesson's treatment of worship as the practical relationship with Allah (images 82-83).

questions.question: Write a note on the effects of belief in Tawheed.
questions.answer: When belief in Allah's oneness is firmly established in the heart, its beneficial effects appear in the personality and practical life. It develops love and respect for Allah, so the servant obeys His commands and avoids His prohibitions, attaining happiness in this world and the Hereafter. It gives man the highest position of freedom and liberty; creates piety, self-control and self-respect; creates humility; and makes him see all creatures with love and affection. It also gives man perseverance, courage, contentment, selflessness, determination, patience and trust by which he copes with life's difficulties, removes despair through belief in Allah's mercy, makes him fearless in doing Jihad to uplift the word of Allah, and creates the idea of the unity and equality of mankind.
questions.explanation: Summarised from the "Effects of Aqeedah-e-Tawheed on Life" section (pages 69-70, images 72-73).

questions.question: "Allah Almighty is eternal". Explain.
questions.answer: Allah Almighty is eternal means He is "the First and the Last" (Surah al-Hadid: 3). Before there was anything, He existed alone, and in the end nothing will remain but He will remain alone. He has always been and will always be; He has neither beginning nor end, and no one has created Him. His attributes are eternal like His Being, and He is Al-Hayy (Ever-Living, Immortal).
questions.explanation: From the first attribute of Allah, "Al-Awwal wal-Akhir" (Everlasting/Eternal), on page 67 (image 70).

questions.question: What does the word "Tawheed" stand for?
questions.answer: Literally, "Tawheed" stands for affirming oneness. In Islamic terminology it stands for the belief that Allah Almighty is One, unique, eternal and incomparable—the sole Creator, Owner and Sovereign of the universe, with no partner, no equal and no precedent—and to believe this with firm conviction of the heart and express it by the tongue when necessary.
questions.explanation: Based on the literal and terminological meaning of Tawheed on page 65 (image 68).

questions.answer: to believe in oneness

questions.question: Write down the literal and terminological meaning and concept of "Risaalat" and "Nubuwwat".
questions.answer: "Nubuwwat" is derived from "Naba", which literally means news, and the one who gives news is called a "Nabi" (Prophet), whose plural is "Ambiyaa" (Prophets). "Risaalat" literally means to convey a message, and the one who conveys the message is called a "Rasool" (Messenger), whose plural is "Rusul" (Messengers). In religious terminology, Prophethood and Apostleship (Nubuwwat and Risaalat) is a high spiritual position on which Allah Almighty has appointed chosen servants from among His servants, through which man attains divine knowledge. It serves as a link between Allah Almighty and His servants: through it Allah conveys His commands and instructions to His servants, and through the Prophets He guides, corrects and trains human beings. The person who holds this position is called a Prophet or a Messenger; even before receiving the divine message, his status in his nation is very high—he is infallible, pious, gentle, virtuous, truthful and trustworthy. In Arabic, "Al-Rasool" specifically refers to the Messenger of Allah (PBUH), and it is obligatory to believe in all the Prophets and Messengers sent by Allah before him.
questions.explanation: Directly from the section "The Literal and Terminological Meaning and Concept of Prophethood and Apostleship" (pages 71-72, images 74-75).

questions.question: Write a note on the belief in Prophethood in detail.
questions.answer: Belief in Prophethood (Nubuwwat) is the second most important and fundamental belief in Islam, and in the chain of Islamic beliefs it comes right after Tawheed (monotheism). It means to believe that Allah Almighty, out of His mercy, appointed chosen servants (Prophets and Messengers) to convey His guidance to mankind through divine revelation. The Holy Qur'an says: "They all believe in Allah, and His angels and His books and His messengers, and they say: We make no distinction among any of His messengers." (Surah Al-Baqarah: 285) Therefore, to believe in all the Prophets and Messengers sent by Allah Almighty before the Holy Prophet (PBUH) is obligatory. The need for Prophethood and Apostleship is evident from several points: (1) Islam states worship and obedience to Allah as the purpose of man's creation, which can occur only through the practical guidance of the Prophets and Messengers; (2) man naturally wants a practical example to mould his life, and the lives of the Prophets are the best practical example; (3) Allah reveals the Book on the Prophet for the guidance of His servants, and the Prophet teaches its teachings, commands and wisdom; (4) the Hereafter is a place of accountability, and without guidance people could plead ignorance on the Day of Resurrection; (5) just as Allah provided all facilities for man's physical needs, He blessed humanity with Prophetic guidance for its spiritual needs. Thus Prophethood is an essential link between Allah and His servants.
questions.explanation: Based on the section "The need for Prophethood and Apostleship" (page 72, image 75) and the Qur'anic verse (Surah Al-Baqarah: 285).

questions.question: Write a note on obedience and following The Holy Prophet (PBUH) in detail.
questions.answer: The word "Ita'at" (obedience) is derived from "Tawun", which literally means heartfelt willingness and obedience. Obedience requires complete surrender; it does not accept obeying some commands while disobeying others. In other words, accepting obedience with a willing heart is called obedience. "Ittiba" (following one's footsteps) means to follow every step and every deed of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) with a deep heartfelt attachment and complete submission. When complete obedience and heartfelt love come together, it is called Ittiba. If someone obeys and follows the commands that the Holy Prophet (PBUH) has ordered or instructed, or his Sunnah in the matters of life, it is called following the footsteps of the Messenger of Allah. The main reason for ordering obedience to the Messenger is that Allah Almighty wants obedience to Him, and the only means of obedience to Allah is the Messenger, because Allah does not speak directly to His slaves but speaks through His Messengers. It is the Messenger who informs people about the instructions and commands of Allah. Therefore obedience to the Messenger is, in fact, obedience to Allah, and whoever wants to obey Allah must obey the Messenger of Allah. Without it, obedience to Allah cannot be imagined, as the Holy Qur'an says: "He who obeys the messenger of Allah, indeed he obeyed Allah." (Surah Al-Nisaa: 80)
questions.explanation: Directly from the section "Obedience and Following to The Holy Prophet" (page 74, image 77), including the Qur'anic verse.

questions.question: Explain the belief in the finality of Prophethood.
questions.answer: The literal meaning of "Khat'm" is to seal, the end of something, and to finish by completing a task. Finality of Prophethood means that the series of Prophethood which started from Hazrat Adam (AS), with many Prophets coming one after another, ended with the Holy Prophet (PBUH). He is the last Prophet of Allah for all human beings till the Day of Resurrection, and now no new Prophet will come. Whoever claims Prophethood in any way after the Holy Prophet (PBUH) is an infidel and is out of the circle of Islam. The Holy Qur'an revealed to the Holy Prophet is the last eternal revelation of Allah to all humanity, after which no other book will be revealed. Allah Almighty says: "Muhammad is not the father of any man among you, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets" (Surah Al-Ahzab: 40), and He also says: "Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My favour upon you, and I have chosen Islam as the religion for you." (Surah Al-Mai'dah: 3) The Holy Prophet (PBUH) said: "There will be among my Ummah thirty great liars, each of them asserting that he is (Allah's) prophet, whereas I am the Last Prophet. After me, there will be no Prophet." (Sunan Abu Dawood: 4252) Thus there is a unanimous consensus of the whole Ummah that the Holy Prophet (PBUH) is the Last Prophet of Allah.
questions.explanation: From the sections "Finality of Prophethood" and "The need for the finality of Prophethood" (pages 75-76, images 76-77).

questions.question: Describe the importance of the love for The Holy Prophet (PBUH) in Islam.
questions.answer: In the light of the Holy Qur'an, there are four essential aspects of our relationship with the Holy Prophet (PBUH): faith, obedience, following his footsteps, and love. Love is the name of a natural attraction and passion, and when it is based on a religious relationship it is called "spiritual love" or "love of faith". The Holy Prophet (PBUH) deserves all kinds of love from us, and this is a requirement of faith because he is the beloved of Allah and the benefactor and mentor of the believers. Therefore Allah Almighty commands us to love His Messenger, and any faith or obedience not based on the love of the Messenger is not valid in the sight of Allah. The requisite of this love is that it should not be merely outward and formal, but a love that overcomes all other loves, in comparison to which even the dearest and most beloved relationship loses its value, and for which everything in the world can be sacrificed. This is the standard of love stated in the Holy Qur'an: "The Prophet has more rights for the believers than their own lives." (Surah Al-Ahzab: 6) In Hadith, the love of the Messenger of Allah is declared a sign of faith: "None of you can be a (true) believer unless he loves me more than his parents, children and all people." (Sahih Bukhari, Book of Iman, Hadith 15)
questions.explanation: From the section "Love for The Holy Prophet" (page 73, image 76), including the Qur'anic and Hadith references.

questions.question: Who is called a Prophet or a Messenger?
questions.answer: The one who receives and gives the news of Allah is called a "Nabi" (Prophet), and the one who conveys the divine message is called a "Rasool" (Messenger). In religious terminology, the chosen servant appointed by Allah Almighty to the high spiritual position of Prophethood and Apostleship—through whom Allah conveys His commands and guidance to His servants—is called a Prophet or a Messenger.
questions.explanation: Based on the definition given on page 71 (image 74).

questions.question: Write down the characteristics of the Prophethood of Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH).
questions.answer: Prophethood started with Prophet Adam (AS) and came to an end on Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH), the Messenger of Allah and the last of all Prophets. The perfections which Allah Almighty bestowed on all previous Prophets individually, He blessed with all of them together in the Shari'ah of the Holy Prophet (PBUH). His Shari'ah has surpassing significance and comprises the excellencies of all previous Prophets' Shari'ahs. Its distinguishing features include generality and universality, abrogation of the first Shari'ah, perfection (preservation of the Divine Book), protection of the Sunnah of the Prophet, comprehensiveness, and finality of Prophethood.
questions.explanation: From the section "Characteristics of the Prophethood of Muhammad" (pages 74-75, images 77-78).

questions.question: What do the Holy Qur'an and Hadith guide us about the finality of Prophethood?
questions.answer: The Holy Qur'an says: "Muhammad is not the father of any man among you, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets (Last of the Prophets)" (Surah Al-Ahzab: 40). The Holy Prophet (PBUH) said: "There will be among my Ummah thirty great liars, each of them asserting that he is (Allah's) prophet, whereas I am the Last Prophet. After me, there will be no Prophet." (Sunan Abu Dawood: 4252) Thus no Prophet will come after him, and there is a unanimous consensus of all the Ummah that the Holy Prophet (PBUH) is the Last Prophet of Allah.
questions.explanation: From the Qur'anic verse and Hadith quoted in the section on the finality of Prophethood (page 76, image 77).

questions.question: What is the sign of perfect faith? Write down.
questions.answer: The sign of perfect faith is the love of the Messenger of Allah. The Holy Prophet (PBUH) said: "None of you can be a (true) believer unless he loves me more than his parents, children and all people." (Sahih Bukhari, Book of Iman, Hadith 15) Thus loving the Holy Prophet (PBUH) more than all other relationships is the sign of perfect faith.

chapters.title: The Importance and Significance of Worship

questions.question: Write a note on "Iba'dat" (worship) in detail.
questions.answer: "Iba'dat" is an Arabic word derived from "Abd". Literally it means worship, humility, submission and obedience. In Islamic terminology, "Iba'dat" means to live according to the blessed life of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) with the intention of gaining the pleasure of Allah Almighty. It includes every action which Allah has commanded to do and abstaining from whatever He has forbidden. Since the servant's job is to obey the master—especially when He is the Master of all the rulers—to consider His commands as a cause of happiness and contentment for oneself is the ascension of a servant. In Islam, after the reformation of faith and belief, the first emphasis is given to worship, because worship is the practical form of direct contact and relationship with Allah Almighty. Allah Almighty says: "And I have not created Jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me." (Surah Al-Zariyat: 56) and "O people! Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you, so that you may save (from His punishment)." (Surah Al-Baqarah: 21) Here worship refers to piety, which is the destination after the purification of the heart and soul and sincerity of action; this condition of a man's heart leads to love for good deeds and hatred of evils.
questions.explanation: From the sections "The meaning and concept of worship" and "The Importance and Significance of Worship" (pages 79-80, images 82-83).

questions.question: Write down the effects of worship on general life.
questions.answer: The Islamic system of worship develops feelings of love and sympathy in man for other human beings; therefore a Muslim loves, sympathizes with, and helps others in their sorrows. Worship also teaches patience and forbearance and awakens the spirit to sacrifice one's own interests for the sake of Allah Almighty and the collective good. It teaches man to live together collectively, so he learns to live with other human beings and becomes a socialist. The punctuality of worship eliminates bad habits like laziness, idleness and wastage of time, and creates in man the qualities of observance of time, outward and inward purification, obedience of a leader and collectivity, so that he abstains from evils and obscenities. Fasting creates piety in man—that is, the fear of Allah Almighty, which helps him distinguish between good and evil. Through paying Zakat the love of wealth decreases within man and he becomes happy to help others financially; Hajj teaches universality; and good deeds like helping people, relating with kin and caring for subordinates improve relationships and affiliations. The correctness of intention and sincerity are the keys to acceptance, and then every good deed has the status of worship for the believer.
questions.explanation: From the section "Effects of Worship on Man's Practical Life" (pages 80-81, images 83-84).

questions.question: Write down the importance and significance of worship.
questions.answer: In Islam, the first emphasis, after the reformation of faith or belief, is given to worship. Worship is the practical form of direct contact and relationship with Allah Almighty, and it is the very purpose of man's creation. Allah Almighty says: "And I have not created Jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me." (Surah Al-Zariyat: 56) and "O people! Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you, so that you may save (from His punishment)." (Surah Al-Baqarah: 21) Every day in every prayer, Muslims repeatedly pray for the straight path, and the verse "And proclaim that my prayers, my sacrifices, and my life and death are all for Allah, the Lord of the worlds" (Surah al-Anaam: 162) gives a brief and comprehensive outline of the straight path, which is the soul of Islamic life and the lifeblood of Islamic society. This verse states that every Muslim's breath, step and deed should be for Allah Almighty's sake alone, not for the other or one's own desire—this is the purpose of a Muslim's life. Thus worship is the means of gaining the pleasure of Allah, of purifying the heart and soul, and of establishing piety, which is the destination of the believer.
questions.explanation: From the sections on the concept and importance of worship (pages 79-80, images 82-83), including the Qur'anic verses cited.

questions.question: What is the literal and terminological meaning of "Iba'dat" (worship)?
questions.answer: Literally, "Iba'dat" (derived from "Abd") means worship, humility, submission and obedience. In Islamic terminology it means to live according to the blessed life of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) with the intention of gaining the pleasure of Allah Almighty, which includes every action Allah has commanded and abstaining from whatever He has forbidden.
questions.explanation: From the definition of worship on page 79 (image 82).

questions.question: Write some requisites of worship.
questions.answer: The requisites of worship are: we should obey all the commands of Allah Almighty and act upon them; we must abstain from what He has made unlawful; we must act upon what He has made obligatory and compulsory with complete obedience; and we should bring every aspect of life under the sphere of obedience to Allah Almighty, as He says: "O Believers! Enter into Islam wholeheartedly." (Surah Al-Baqarah: 208) The correctness of intention and sincerity are also the keys to the acceptance of worship.

questions.question: Explain the significance and importance of Jihad.
questions.answer: Islam has given much importance to Jihad because only through Jihad is it possible to create an atmosphere of peace and security in the world and to protect human rights by eliminating distortion, corruption, oppression and all kinds of evil deeds which cause conflict and disorder in society. Allah Almighty says: "And do Jihad in the way of Allah with your wealth and your lives, it is better for you if you knew." (Surah Al-Tawbah: 41) Regarding the emphasis on Jihad, the Messenger of Allah (PBUH) said: "One who died in a state that he did not fight in the way of Allah practically nor did he express any desire (or determination) for Jihad, so he died the death of a hypocrite." (Sahih Muslim: 1910) Thus Jihad is a great duty that establishes peace, promotes goodness and virtue, eliminates evils and vices from society, protects human rights, and defends the religion, life, property and honour of the Muslims.
questions.explanation: From the section "The significance and importance of Jihad" (page 82, image 85), including the Qur'anic verse and the Hadith.

questions.question: Describe the types of Jihad.
questions.answer: According to the lesson, the types of Jihad and its practical forms are three. (1) Jihad against the desires of the self: the inner strength that prevents man from obeying and worshipping Allah is the soul which enjoins evil and incites man to commit sins and disobedience, including selfishness, hatred, backbiting, lies, vulgar talking and other self-desires; the domination of these desires corrupts human actions and character. Overcoming this enjoin-er of evils falls into the category of Jihad. Allah says: "And for one who fears to stand before his Lord and restrains his soul from evil desire, then indeed Paradise only is his destination." (Surah al-Nazi'at: 40-41) The Holy Prophet (PBUH) declared a person who controls his self to be a Mujahid: "A Mujahid is one who strives against his own soul (regarding obedience to Allah)." (Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 1621) In some traditions, striving against one's soul is declared the biggest Jihad (Jihad-e-Akbar). (2) Jihad to eradicate evils: when individual evils prevail commonly in a society they take the form of collective evils, which Islam names Munkaraat. Islam not only rejects every action that causes trouble in society but commands believers to eradicate it, so that the social order remains peaceful and organized. The Prophet (PBUH) said: "He who sees something evil amongst you should change it with the help of his hand; and if he has not strength enough to do it, then he should do it with his tongue, and if he has not strength enough, then he should dislike it from his heart." (Sahih Muslim: 49) It is the responsibility of the government to eradicate evils with force, of the scholars and writers to forbid them with tongue and pen, and of every individual to consider evil as vicious and avoid it. The best Jihad is to speak a word of justice in front of a tyrant ruler (Sunan Abu Dawood: 4344). (3) Jihad by the sword / Armed Jihad (Fighting): if an enemy force invades an Islamic country, then it becomes obligatory on it to fight and protect its borders, religion, faith, life and property, and the honour and dignity of its citizens.
questions.explanation: From the section "Types of Jihad and its Practical Forms" (pages 82-84, images 85-87), which enumerates jihad against the self, jihad to eradicate evils, and armed jihad.

questions.question: Write down the conditions for Jihad.
questions.answer: Islam has laid down certain conditions for armed Jihad which should be kept in view while doing Jihad. (A) For the exaltation of the religion of Allah: the first condition is that armed Jihad should be only for the exaltation of the religion of Allah. (B) Declaration by the Islamic State: the second condition is that the state should make a declaration of war; in Islam only the state has the authority to declare war, so the declaration of an individual or a group, or issuing a Fatwa, has no value in Shariah for waging war—rather such Fatwa or declarations fall into the category of mischief on earth. (C) Adequate availability of military power: the government should have adequate power and strength to fight the opposing force, and the Holy Qur'an emphasizes keeping the Islamic state strong: "Prepare (as much as possible) against them what you can of military power and cavalry to deter Allah's enemies and your enemies..." (Surah al-Anfaal: 60) The meaning is that Muslims should always be ready with the equipment of war and a permanent army to take immediate action in case of need and fight the enemy to the fullest. (D) Methods of ignorance should not be used in war: the fight should be against those who are armed in battle and ready to fight; women, children, the elderly, the wounded and civilians should not be attacked, and the victims of the enemies should not be cut off their ears and noses, nor should fields, houses and livestock be destroyed without any reason.
questions.explanation: From the section "Conditions of armed Jihad" (pages 87-88, images 90-91).

questions.question: What is the meaning and concept of Jihad?
questions.answer: Jihad is an Arabic word derived from "Juh'd". It literally means hard work, striving hard, doing the utmost hard and endeavour. In Islamic Shariah, Jihad means to make every effort and endeavour for the sake of Allah Almighty, which is for the upliftment, protection and defence of the country and nation; and also every effort and endeavour for the reformation of society—to promote goodness and virtue and eliminate evils and vices from society.
questions.explanation: From the section "Meaning and concept of Jihad" and its Shariah term (page 82, image 85).

questions.question: Explain the objectives of Jihad.
questions.answer: Besides defending and protecting the Islamic state, the Holy Qur'an describes other objectives of armed Jihad: (A) Punishment for breaking the agreement—Islam commands fighting against a nation that makes an agreement with the Islamic government not to wage war but has intentions of war behind that agreement, for Allah does not like the treacherous; the command is general though its background was a special occasion. (B) Respect for humanity and helping the oppressed—the Islamic government must support and help the oppressed and rid them of the oppressor's oppression, as stated in Surah Al-Nisa: 75 concerning oppressed men, women and children. (C) Elimination of sedition and mischief—wherever a government or group attacks the weak for its evil purposes and inflicts oppression and mischief, the Qur'an urges the Islamic State to wage war against them until there is no more persecution and the religion is entirely for Allah (Surah al-Baqarah: 193).
questions.explanation: From the section "The objectives of the armed Jihad" (pages 86-87, images 89-90).

questions.question: Write an article on the commencement of Prophethood.
questions.answer: The commencement (advent) of Prophethood is the great turning point in human history. Before it, the whole world, and particularly Arabia, was sunk in ignorance, idolatry and moral corruption. The Holy Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) was born in Makkah and, as he grew up, he was known among his people as Sadiq (truthful) and Amin (trustworthy). When he reached the age of forty, he was, as usual, engaged in worship in the solitude of the Cave of Hira during the month of Ramadan. One day the angel Jibraeel (A.S) came to him by the command of Allah Almighty and lit the light of Prophethood which was hidden in his blessed chest with the words of divine revelation. The first five verses of Surah Al-Alaq were revealed to him. By this revelation the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) was exalted to the proclamation of Prophethood and Apostleship. This Prophethood is the last and its Shariah is the last Shariah. From this point the mission of the last Prophethood started and the revelations began.
questions.explanation: Grounded in lesson 3.C.1, which describes the Cave of Hira, the descent of angel Jibraeel, the first five verses of Surah Al-Alaq and the Prophet being raised to the last Prophethood in the month of Ramadan.

questions.question: Write down the situations of Arab before the commencement of Prophethood.
questions.answer: Before the commencement of Prophethood, Makkah had become the largest city in Arabia and the spiritual and social centre of the Quraysh. Due to its commerce, culture and development it was equal to Sana'a of Yemen, and its caravans travelled twice a year to Syria and Yemen. Its administrative structure, established by Qu'sai Bin Kilab in the fifth century A.D., was based on unity, cooperation and the mutual division of administrative matters, and a consultative council called Dar al-Nadwah was set up to resolve war, trade and social issues. However, because of the city's wealth many families had become rich and capitalist. Some were charitable and helped the needy, but others were luxurious, stubborn, harsh on the weak and proud of their wealth and children; they looked down upon others. Evils such as drinking alcohol, oppression, immorality, obscenity, robbery, theft and gambling were not considered abominable, and teasing neighbours, breaking ties of kin and shedding unjust blood were their hobbies. In the rest of Hijaz the people had become rebellious due to mismanagement and displacement, killing and fighting with their own people was considered courage and pride, and they felt proud to bury their daughters alive. Idolatry had become their religious motto and 360 idols were placed inside the Ka'ba alone. Allah Almighty described this state in the Holy Qur'an: 'There was corruption in the land and in the sea' (Surah al-Rome: 41).
questions.explanation: Grounded in lesson 3.C.1, which surveys the social, economic, moral and religious conditions of pre-Islamic Arabia, including Makkah's prosperity, Dar al-Nadwah and the 360 idols of the Ka'ba.

questions.question: Mention the objectives of the commencement of Prophethood.
questions.answer: The objectives of the commencement of Prophethood are stated by Allah Almighty in Surah Al-Jumu'ah (verse 2). Four points were made the axis and centre of the Prophet's mission: (1) To recite and read the verses of Allah Almighty to the people; (2) to purify them; (3) to teach them the Book (the Holy Qur'an); and (4) to teach them the words of wisdom. In other words, the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) was the preacher who recited the verses of Allah Almighty, the teacher who taught those verses, the guide who made the verses understood, and the reformer who himself complied with the verses. The mention of 'reading' and the 'pen' in the first revelation indicates the importance of learning and knowledge in the objectives of this Prophethood.
questions.explanation: Grounded in lesson 3.C.1, which cites Surah Al-Jumu'ah: 2 to list the four objectives (reciting the verses, purification, teaching the Book and teaching wisdom).

questions.question: Write the translation of the verses of the first revelation.
questions.answer: The translation of the five verses of the first revelation (Surah Al-Alaq: 1-5) is as follows: '1. Read with the name of your Lord Who created. 2. Created man from a clot. 3. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, 4. Who taught knowledge with the pen. 5. Taught man that which he knew not.'
questions.explanation: Directly quoted from the translation of Surah Al-Alaq: 1-5 given in the first revelation (lesson 3.C.1).

questions.question: Explain the concept of the commencement of Prophethood.
questions.answer: The commencement (beginning) of Prophethood means the occasion when Allah Almighty raised the Holy Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) to Prophethood. When he reached the age of forty, he was worshipping in the solitude of the Cave of Hira in the month of Ramadan. The angel Jibraeel (A.S) came to him by the command of Allah and lit the light of Prophethood hidden in his blessed chest with the words of divine revelation, and he was exalted to the proclamation of Prophethood and Apostleship. With this, the last Prophethood and the last Shariah began and the revelations started.
questions.explanation: Based on the section 'The Meaning of the commencement of Prophethood' in lesson 3.C.1.

questions.question: Outline the four points mentioned in the Holy Quran about the objectives of the Prophethood.
questions.answer: The four points mentioned in the Holy Qur'an (Surah Al-Jumu'ah: 2) about the objectives of the Prophethood are: (1) to recite and read the verses of Allah Almighty to the people; (2) to purify them; (3) to teach them the Book (the Holy Qur'an); and (4) to teach them the words of wisdom.

questions.question: Write a note on the stages of invitation and preaching.
questions.answer: The Holy Prophet (S.A.W) invited and preached Islam in three stages during his Makkan life. (1) The first stage was secret preaching. For three years after the revelation the Prophet (S.A.W) preached Tawheed with silence and secrecy, working first on family members and trusted friends. As a result Hazrat Abu Bakr (R.A) was the first among men, Hazrat Khadija (R.A) among women, Zaid bin Haritha (R.A) among slaves and Hazrat Ali (R.A) among children to embrace Islam. The house of Hazrat Arqam (R.A), called 'Dar-e-Arqam', situated on Safa Hill, became the centre of their gatherings where the Muslims learned the teachings of the Holy Qur'an and offered prayers; hence it became the first centre of invitation and preaching in Makkah. Allah Almighty instructed the Prophet (S.A.W) at the time of the second revelation: 'O the Cloaked One! Rise up and warn! And proclaim the Greatness of your Lord' (Surah al-Muddaththir: 1-3). (2) The second stage was open preaching. After three years the command of Allah came: 'And (O dear Prophet) warn your closest relatives' (Surah al-Shuara: 214). The Holy Prophet (S.A.W) invited the family of Abdul Muttalib to a feast and asked who among them would support him in this holy campaign; the whole gathering remained silent and only the young Hazrat Ali Murtaza (R.A) stood up and promised support. Then, on the hill of Safa, the Prophet (S.A.W) called the people of Quraysh by the names of their tribes and proclaimed: 'Say: There is none worthy of worship except Allah. You will be successful'; but his uncle Abu Lahab was the first to reject him. (3) In the third stage Allah Almighty gave this message to the whole human race: 'And We have sent for the whole humanity as a giver of glad tidings and a warner' (Surah Sabaa: 28). The Messenger of Allah continued his campaign by visiting the seasonal markets of Arabia such as O'kaz, Majna and Zul-Mijaz and delivered the message of Islam, and he also went to Ta'if to preach Islam, remaining busy inviting people to Allah for about ten days.
questions.explanation: Grounded in lesson 3.C.2, which describes the three stages of Makkan preaching: secret preaching, open preaching and invitation to the whole of humanity.

questions.question: Explain the principles of invitation and preaching.
questions.answer: The principles of invitation and preaching are stated in the Holy Qur'an: 'Call people to the path of your Lord with wisdom and kind advice and debate within a better way' (Surah Al-Nahal: 125). From this verse three principles are derived. (1) Preaching with wisdom: the talk should be according to the level and mental capacity of the addressee, willingness to listen should be created, and the reasoning should be scientific and rational according to the situation and occasion. (2) Kind advice: there is definitely an effect of speaking in a good manner; to speak effectively by showing the good and the bad in front of the addressee, so that no one is hurt and everyone is convinced of the truth, is termed kind advice. (3) Debate and discussion: if a situation of discussion or dialogue arises, it should be full of arguments and the language should be good and polite in order to disprove the opponent's opinion; while talking, anger, excitement and screaming should be avoided, and there should be understanding and convincing. It is also essential for the preacher to act on what he preaches, as Allah Almighty says: 'And who is better in speech than he who calls (people) to Allah and does good deeds' (Surah Fussilat: 33).
questions.explanation: Grounded in lesson 3.C.2, which derives the three principles of wisdom, kind advice and best-manner debate from Surah Al-Nahal: 125.

questions.question: Describe the meaning and concept of invitation and preaching.
questions.answer: Literally, 'Da'wah' in Arabic means to call and to invite, while 'Tab'ligh' means to convey. In Islamic terminology, to call people to Islam and to invite them to good deeds and religious education is called 'Da'wah of Religion', and to convey these teachings to other people, nations and countries with the spirit of benevolence is called 'Tab'ligh'. Allah Almighty says: 'And who is better in speech than he who calls to Allah and does good deeds' (Surah Fussilat: 33).
questions.explanation: Based on the section 'The meaning of invitation (Da'wah) and preaching (Tab'ligh)' in lesson 3.C.2.

questions.question: What are the objectives of invitation and preaching?
questions.answer: The primary objectives of invitation and preaching are: to convey the message of Allah Almighty to the people; to believe in Allah Almighty as the One God and Lord and not to associate anyone with Him, His attributes, authorities and rights; to consider Islam as the religion of truth and to consider oneself accountable before Allah Almighty; to believe in all the Prophets of Allah completely and follow their footsteps; to believe that Prophet Muhammad (S.A.W) is the Messenger of Allah and the last of all the Prophets; and to encourage the promotion of goodness by following his Seerah and to encourage the eradication of evils.
questions.explanation: Based on the section 'Purposes of Invitation and Preaching' in lesson 3.C.2.

questions.question: Briefly describe the effects of invitation and preaching.
questions.answer: The effects of invitation and preaching were far-reaching. In the beginning Suwaid bin Samit, an Ansar of Medina famous for bravery and poetry, came to Makkah during the Hajj period and, after hearing a few verses of the Qur'an from the Prophet (S.A.W), was convinced of the reality of Islam. His conversion affected other people of Medina and many embraced Islam within two or three years, after which the migration of Muslims from Makkah to Medina began and the Muslims became strong. The Prophet (S.A.W) too migrated to Medina, laid the foundation of a mosque and made agreements with the tribes of Medina and its surroundings. After the battles of Badr, Uhud and the Trench and the treaty of Hudaybiya, he wrote letters of invitation to the kings; Khyber was conquered and finally Makkah was conquered. On the occasion of the Farewell Hajj more than one lac companions prepared for Hajj.
questions.explanation: Based on the section 'Effects and Fruits of Invitation and preaching' in lesson 3.C.2.

questions.question: What do you know about the event of migration? Explain.
questions.answer: The event of migration (Hijrat) is one of the most important events of Islamic history. As the oppression of the polytheists increased and the environment of Medina became favourable, the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) permitted the Muslims to migrate to Medina on the 27th of Safar in the thirteenth year of Prophethood. When the leaders of the Quraysh saw the Muslims living in peace in Medina and the powerful tribes of Aws and Khaz'raj as their helpers, they gathered in Dar al-Nadwa and plotted against the Holy Prophet (S.A.W). Allah Almighty informed him of this plot. He called Hazrat Ali (R.A) and told him to sleep on his bed wearing his shawl, and in the morning to hand over the trusts of the disbelievers to their owners and then reach Medina. The Holy Prophet (S.A.W), taking Hazrat Abu Bakr (R.A) with him, left Makkah in the darkness of night, addressing the city with love and saying that he would not have left had his people not forced him out, and went to Mount Thaur. Both stayed in the Cave of Thaur for three days, during which Hazrat Abdullah, the young son of Hazrat Abu Bakr, informed them about the conditions of the whole day and night, Aa'mir bin Fuhairah gave him milk while grazing goats, and Hazrat Asma (R.A), the eldest daughter of Abu Bakr, brought cooked food. On the fourth day they came out of the cave and hired Abdullah bin Ariqat as a guide, and the caravan moved day and night. On the way, at noon due to the heat, Hazrat Abu Bakr looked around, saw a shadow near a mound and camped there, and brought milk from a shepherd for the Prophet (S.A.W). They reached the town of Quba safely in the fourteenth year of Prophethood, 1st A.H., where the Prophet (S.A.W) stayed a few days, built the Mosque of Quba and offered prayers in it. He left for Medina and, offering Friday prayers in the valley of Banu Sa'lim bin Awf, reached Medina on Friday, where the people received him warmly, expressed happiness over his arrival and generously cooperated with him.
questions.explanation: Grounded in lesson 3.C.3, which narrates the plot in Dar al-Nadwa, the stay in the Cave of Thaur, the guide and helpers, and the arrival at Quba and Medina.

questions.question: Explain the reasons for migration to Medina.
questions.answer: The reasons for migration to Medina are as follows. (i) Prohibition of the Da'wah of Islam in Makkah: before the proclamation of Prophethood the Quraysh called the Prophet (S.A.W) by the titles of Sadiq (truthful) and Amin (trustworthy), but after the proclamation of Prophethood they became his mortal enemies, so it became very challenging for him to invite people to Islam. (ii) Violence against Muslims: in Makkah the enemies inflicted atrocities on every convert to Islam and left no opportunity to inflict physical or mental torture on them; they even besieged the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) and other Muslims for three years in Sha'b Abi Talib with a complete social boycott, and tortured and martyred many companions. (iii) The encouraging experience of emigration to Abyssinia: due to the harsh attitude of the Quraysh the companions were forced to migrate twice to Abyssinia, where they found peace and comfort, though on account of the conspiracies of the opponents they returned to Makkah and continued to bear the persecutions of the infidels. (iv) The eagerness of the people of Medina: some noble people of Medina had twice pledged allegiance to the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) at the palace of Aqaba and invited him to come to Medina and teach them the teachings of Islam. (v) Divine permission: keeping in view all these difficulties and at the insistence of the Muslims, the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) allowed the Muslims to migrate to Medina on the 27th of Safar in the thirteenth year of Prophethood, and this migration became obligatory for all Muslims.
questions.explanation: Grounded in lesson 3.C.3, which lists five reasons for the migration to Medina under headings (i) to (v).

questions.question: Write down the brief introduction of "Gazwaat" (battles).
questions.answer: 'Ghazwa' literally means going out to fight, attacking and fighting. According to the narrators of Hadith and the Seerah writers, a 'Ghazwa' is a war campaign in which the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) himself participated, and as the commander of the army he strove for the exaltation of the religion of Allah Almighty. After the migration, all the Arab tribes were ready to attack Medina and the Quraysh conspired with the Jews of Medina and sent threatening messages, so Allah Almighty permitted the Muslims to wage Jihad in self-defence, saying: 'Permission is granted to those against whom the disbelievers wage war because they are being wronged; and indeed Allah has power to help them' (Surah al-Hajj: 39). In order to defend the state of Medina the Messenger of Allah waged Jihad against the opponents of Islam, and some of the important battles are: the Battle of Badr (2nd A.H., Ramadan) in which 313 Muslims defeated 1000 infidels under Abu Jahl; the Battle of Uhud (3rd A.H., Shawwal) against Abu Sufyan; the Battle of the Trench or Ah'zaab (5th A.H., Zul-Qa'd); the Battle of Khyber (7th A.H.) in which the fort of Qamoos was conquered under Hazrat Ali (R.A); the Conquest of Makkah (8th A.H., Ramadan); the Battle of Hunain (8th A.H.); and the Battle of Tabuk (9th A.H.) where the Romans did not turn up and the Muslim army returned without any fight.
questions.explanation: Grounded in lesson 3.C.3, which defines 'Ghazwa' and lists the major battles from Badr to Tabuk.

questions.question: What is the meaning and concept of "Hijrat" (migration)?
questions.answer: Literally, 'Hijrat' means taking apart, separating and migrating from one place to another. In Islam it means to leave one's original homeland and home and settle in another country in order to gain the pleasure of Allah Almighty, especially where Muslims are subjugated and oppressed and are in difficulty in living according to Islam; then they should move to a place where they can meet the requirements of the religion and it is easy to follow Islam. Those who migrated from Makkah are called 'Muhajir' and the people of Medina who helped them are called 'Ansar'.
questions.explanation: Based on the section 'The meaning and concept of migration' in lesson 3.C.3.

questions.question: When and why did the battle of Bad'r occur?
questions.answer: The Battle of Badr occurred in the 2nd A.H. during the month of Ramadan. The Holy Prophet (S.A.W) had completed one year in Medina when the polytheists of Makkah, under the command of Abu Jahl, intended to attack Medina. When the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) received this information he went ahead and confronted the polytheists at the place of Badr, and Allah Almighty granted victory to the Muslims.
questions.explanation: Based on the section 'Battle of Badr' in lesson 3.C.3.

questions.question: Write a note on the virtue of migration.
questions.answer: The virtue of migration is very great: the immigrant Muslims got benefits in this world and in the Hereafter and are entitled to the mercy of Allah Almighty. For them are forgiveness, Paradise and the best reward, and they are assured that their deeds will not go in vain. Allah Almighty says: 'So their Lord accepted their prayer, for I do not waste the efforts of any (righteous) worker, male or female ... so those who migrated for Me and were driven out from their homes and were harassed in My cause, and (in the way of Allah) fought, and were martyred - I will certainly wipe out all their sins and will certainly admit them into Gardens beneath which rivers flow; a reward from Allah; and only with Allah is the best reward' (Surah Aal Imran: 195). The condition, however, is that the migration should be in the way of Allah Almighty and one should remain steadfast on His religion for its invitation and preaching.
questions.explanation: Based on the section 'The virtue of migration' in lesson 3.C.3, which cites Surah Aal Imran: 195.

questions.question: The literal meaning of "Hijrat" is:
questions.answer: c
questions.explanation: The lesson defines Hijrat as leaving one's homeland and settling elsewhere to gain the pleasure of Allah, i.e. migrating for the sake of religion.

questions.optionsRaw: (a) to be a Muslim (b) to travel for seeking knowledge (c) to migrate from somewhere for the sake of religion (d) to stay

questions.answer: b
questions.explanation: The lesson states that the Holy Prophet and Hazrat Abu Bakr stayed in the Cave of Thaur for three days during the migration.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) the cave of Hira (b) the cave of Thaur (c) the cave (d) Ta'if

questions.answer: c
questions.explanation: A 'Ghazwa' is defined as a war campaign in which the Holy Prophet himself participated as commander; a campaign he did not personally join is called a Sar'ya.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Booty (b) Jiz'ya (c) Gazwah (d) Sar'ya

chapters.title: Qualities and Characteristics of The Holy Prophet (S.A.W)

questions.question: Write down the importance and virtue of the qualities and characteristics of The Holy Prophet (S.A.W).
questions.answer: The qualities (Khasa'il) and characteristics (Shama'il) of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) have great importance and virtue. The blessed life of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) is the only right and perfect picture of Islam, and following his sayings, deeds and life is the saviour for the believers. Allah Almighty says: '(O Muslims!) In fact, there is an excellent practical example for you in the Messenger of Allah' (Surah al-Ahzaab: 21), and He has declared the excellent habits and unique biography of His Beloved Prophet as the best practical example of 'Uswa-e-Hasana'. Allah Almighty made the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) a combination of high character, high morals and excellent attributes, and the Holy Qur'an itself testifies: 'Of course, your morals are very high' (Surah al-Qalam: 4). The Messenger of Allah was the most perfect both in character and appearance - the most benevolent, the most virtuous, the most honest, the most generous, the most pious and the most faithful. Therefore, whoever wants to make his individual and collective life beautiful and successful should follow these qualities and characteristics with full readiness and heartfelt attachment. Believers must know his commandments, his likes and dislikes, his style of sitting, standing and conversation, his way of walking and dressing and his favourite food; only after knowing all this can they follow the Sunnah of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) and attain salvation in both worlds.
questions.explanation: Grounded in lesson 3.C.4, which explains the importance of the Prophet's Khasa'il and Shama'il with reference to Surah al-Ahzaab: 21 and Surah al-Qalam: 4.

questions.question: What was the way of The Holy Prophet (S.A.W) in helping the people?
questions.answer: The Holy Prophet's way of helping the people was most compassionate and benevolent, and in it the poor and weak were treated in the same way as the wealthy. He would listen to the cries of the oppressed and the helpless and would help them, and this was his favourite hobby. Once a stranger came to the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) and complained that Abu Jahl owed him a debt and was not paying it. At that time the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) was busy in worship in the Haram of Makkah, but he postponed the worship, stood up and went to his enemy Abu Jahl to help the stranger, and received the recovered right from him on the stranger's behalf (Tahzeeb Seerat Ibn Hisham, p. 74). In the 8th A.H., when Allah Almighty granted him victory over the Quraysh and Makkah was conquered, instead of taking revenge for all the atrocities and excesses of the twenty years he forgave his nation and declared: 'There is no blame on you today, go, for you are all free' (Rahmatul Lilaalameen, vol: 1, p: 113). Thus the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) helped people irrespective of their status and even forgave his enemies.
questions.explanation: Grounded in lesson 3.C.4, which narrates the incident of the stranger and Abu Jahl's debt and the Prophet's general amnesty at the conquest of Makkah.

questions.question: What do the "Khasa'il" and "Shama'il" of The Holy Prophet (S.A.W) mean?
questions.answer: 'Khasa'il' is derived from the Arabic word 'Khas'lat', which means habits (good or bad), while 'Shama'il' is the plural of 'Shamila', which means good nature, good habits and good qualities. The Khasa'il and Shama'il of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) refer to his outward and inward qualities, his good habits and his daily routines of nights and days, such as standing, sitting, eating, drinking, sleeping, waking up, temperament, sociability, dressing, morals, blessed qualities and attributes, his treatment with his family members, his interaction with people, his attitude towards his companions, and his blessed appearance and physical constitution.
questions.explanation: Based on the section 'Meaning and concept of Khasa'il and Shama'il' in lesson 3.C.4.

questions.question: What were the domestic routines of The Holy Prophet (S.A.W)?
questions.answer: The domestic life of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) was very polite and pleasant. He helped his family with household works, did his own work himself and never treated his family harshly. He used to take care of his garments, milk his sheep and take care of his own needs; he would patch his garments, sew and mend his shoes and sew his clothes, and he did all these himself (Musnad Ahmad, Hadith: 25341). Hazrat Ayesha (R.A) narrates that the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) said: 'The best of you is the one who is best for his family, and I am the best of you in the matter of my family' (Sunan Tirmizi: 3895). He also used to greet his family when entering the house, and treating the family with good manners and meeting their needs plays an important role in building a better family.
questions.explanation: Based on the section 'The Treatment of The Holy Prophet with his family' in lesson 3.C.4.

questions.question: What kind of attitude does the blessed life of The Holy Prophet (S.A.W) teach towards the people of the neighbourhood?
questions.answer: The blessed life of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) teaches an attitude of good morals and manners towards the people of the neighbourhood in order to create the best possible society and promote mutual harmony. It teaches that relatives and neighbours should be treated well, their needs should be taken care of, gifts should be sent to them, they should be treated with kindness, condolences should be offered, they should be invited and visited, the poor people of the society should be served, and even enemies should be treated well. Hazrat Khadija (R.A), addressing the Holy Prophet (S.A.W), said that he keeps good relations with his kin, helps the poor and the destitute, serves guests generously and assists the calamity-afflicted ones (Sahih Bukhari: Kitab Bad Al-Wahi: 2).
questions.explanation: Based on the section 'The Behaviour of The Holy Prophet with the People of the Society' in lesson 3.C.4.

questions.question: The "Khasa'il" and "Shama'il" of The Holy Prophet mean:
questions.answer: d
questions.explanation: Khasa'il means habits and Shama'il means good nature, good habits and good qualities of the Holy Prophet.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Seerah of the Prophet (b) Uswa-e-Hasana (c) Sunnah (d) good habits and qualities

questions.question: On the occasion of the conquest of Makkah, all the people of Makkah were:
questions.answer: c
questions.explanation: At the conquest of Makkah the Holy Prophet declared, 'There is no blame on you today, go, for you are all free', forgiving his nation instead of taking revenge.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) made prisoners. (b) compelled to leave the city (c) forgiven by The Holy Prophet (d) made leaders.

questions.question: When The Holy Prophet went to the Jewish boy, so he:
questions.answer: a
questions.explanation: The Holy Prophet visited a sick Jewish boy and invited him to Islam, and the boy accepted; this reflects his compassion and his mission of invitation and preaching extended to all people.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) invited him to Islam. (b) greeted him. (c) gifted him something. (d) prayed for him.

questions.question: Describe the love of the Holy Prophet (سم الله عليه وآله واصحابه وسلم) for his household in the light of Ahadith.
questions.answer: The Holy Prophet (PBUH) had deep and immense love for his household (Ahl-e-Bait), and many Ahadith describe this love. He declared: "I have left among you two things. As long as you are attached to them, you can never get astray. It is the Book of Allah and my household (Ahl-e-Bait)." (Sunan Tirmizi: 3786). Hazrat Ayesha reports that the Holy Prophet once called Hazrat Fatima Al-Zahra, Hazrat Ali, Hazrat Hassan and Hazrat Hussain, covered them with a mantle and prayed: "O Allah! These are my household, remove impurity from them and make them pure." (Hadith al-Kisa). Whenever he passed by the house of Hazrat Fatima on his way to prayer, he used to call: "Namaz, O household, may Allah remove impurity from you." (Sunan Tirmizi: 3206). About his grandsons he said: "These two (Hassan and Hussain) are my sons. I love them, O Allah! Love them and also those who love them." (Sunan Tirmizi: 3775). About Hazrat Fatima he said: "Fatima is a part of me, and he who makes her angry, makes me angry." Hazrat Abu Hurairah reports that the Holy Prophet said: "The best among you is he who takes care of my household after me." Thus his love for his household was a model of affection and honour which all Muslims are commanded to follow.
questions.explanation: Drawn from the lesson text which cites Sunan Tirmizi (3786, 3206, 3775), Sahih al-Bukhari and Hadith al-Kisa describing the Prophet's love for Ahl-e-Bait.

questions.question: What do you know about the Mothers of Faithful?
questions.answer: The wives of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) are titled "Ummahat ul Muminen" (the mothers of all believers), as Allah Almighty says: "And the wives of the Prophet are the mothers of the believers." (Surah Al-Ahzab: 6). Their number is eleven; two of them died during the lifetime of the Holy Prophet and nine lived with him until the last days of his life. The most prominent among them are: (1) Umm Al-Mu'minin Hazrat Khadija bint Khuwailad (RA) — the first woman to believe in the Holy Prophet, whom he married when she was 40; all his offspring, except Hazrat Ibrahim, were from her; she dedicated all her wealth to Islam and passed away at the age of 60 in the 10th year of Prophethood. (2) Umm Al-Mu'minin Hazrat Ayesha Siddiqa (RA) bint Abu Bakr Siddique — married in Shawwal 11th year of Prophethood, one of the most prominent jurist women of the Ummah, very brave and courageous; she healed the wounds of the Prophet in the Battle of Uhud and passed away on 17th Ramadan, 57 A.H., buried in Jannat-ul-Baqi. (3) Hazrat Zainab bint Khuzaima (RA), called "Umm Al-Masakin" (Mother of the poor) because she fed the poor very much. (4) Hazrat Zainab bint Jahash (RA), a very pious and generous woman who died at 53 in 20 A.H. The other purified wives are Hazrat Sawda bint Zama'ah, Hazrat Hafsa bint Umar bin Khattab, Hazrat Umm-e-Salma bint Abu Umayyah, Hazrat Juwairiya bint Al-Harith, Hazrat Umm-e-Habiba Ram'la bint Abu Sufyan, Hazrat Safia bint Huyai bin Akh'tab, Hazrat Maimuna bint Harith, and Hazrat Maria Qibtia (RA) (sent as a gift by Muqawqas, the King of Egypt, and mother of Hazrat Ibrahim). Allah also addressed them: "O wives of the Prophet! You are not like the ordinary women of the world..." (Surah Al-Ahzab: 32). All his purified wives are the family members and the beacons of guidance for the Muslim Ummah.
questions.explanation: Based on the lesson section "The Purified wives", listing the Ummahat ul Muminen and the Qur'anic verse of Surah Al-Ahzab (6 and 32).

questions.question: What is meant by 'Manaqib'?
questions.answer: The word "Manaqib" is an Arabic word; its singular is "Manqabat", which means praise, good deeds, qualities and virtues. In technical terms, the achievements and virtues of a famous personality are called "Manqabat", whether in prose or poetry — such as the praise, qualities and virtues of Ahl-e-Bait Athar, religious leaders and the companions.
questions.explanation: Definition taken directly from the opening section "The meaning and concept of the word Manaqib".

questions.question: Who are Ahl e Bait?
questions.answer: The word "Ahl" in Arabic means eligible or member, and "Bayt" means "home", so Ahl al-Bayt means family. According to the Qur'anic term, "Ahl-e-Bayt" refers to the family of the Holy Prophet (PBUH), which includes his wives and children. The Holy Qur'an has declared his wives as "Ummahat ul Muminen" (the mothers of all believers). In the light of Hadith al-Kisa and Surah Al-Ahzab (33), the Ahl-e-Bait include the Holy Prophet, his purified wives, his offspring, Hazrat Ali, Hazrat Fatima Al-Zahra, Hazrat Hassan and Hazrat Hussain.
questions.explanation: Compiled from the lesson's definition of Ahl-e-Bayt and the Hadith al-Kisa passage on images 121-122.

questions.question: Write down the rights of Ahl e Bait.
questions.answer: The rights of the household of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) are: (1) We must love them. (2) We must obey them. (3) We must believe in their justness. (4) We must love those who love them and detest those who keep hatred for them. We should also develop immense love for the Ahl-e-Bait, abide by their teachings and follow their footsteps so that we may gain the nearness of the Holy Prophet and his intercession on the Day of Judgement.
questions.explanation: Listed explicitly in the lesson under the heading "Rights of Ahl e Bait".

questions.question: Outline the names of Ahl e Bait in the light of Hadith al-Kisa.
questions.answer: According to Hadith al-Kisa, Hazrat Ayesha reports that the Holy Prophet (PBUH) called upon Hazrat Fatima Al-Zahra, Hazrat Ali, Hazrat Hassan and Hazrat Hussain, and covered them with a mantle and prayed: "O Allah! These are my household, remove impurity from them and make them pure." Thus the Ahl-e-Bait named in Hadith al-Kisa are Hazrat Fatima Al-Zahra, Hazrat Ali, Hazrat Hassan and Hazrat Hussain, together with the Holy Prophet himself.
questions.explanation: Taken from the passage describing Hadith al-Kisa in the lesson.

questions.question: The wives of the Holy Prophet (سم الله عليه وآله واصحابه وسلم) are titled in the Holy Quran as:
questions.answer: Ummahat ul Mominen (the mothers of the believers), as declared in Surah Al-Ahzab: 6.
questions.explanation: The Qur'an says "And the wives of the Prophet are the mothers of the believers" (Surah Al-Ahzab: 6), so option (a) is correct.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Ummahat ul Mominen (b) Ummahat ul Muslimeen (c) Akhwat ul Momineen (d) Sayyedat ul Muslimen

questions.answer: The household, because "Ahl" means member/family and "Bayt" means home.
questions.explanation: The lesson states "Ahl" means eligible or member and "Bayt" means home, so Ahl al-Bayt literally means the household (family). Hence option (c) is correct.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Those who write about home (b) Poets (c) The household (d) Faithful

chapters.title: Greatness of Companions and The Ten Blessed

questions.question: Write down a note on the excellence of companions.
questions.answer: By virtue of the blessed company of the Holy Prophet (PBUH), the companions (Sahaba) achieved a high status and excellence that anyone afterwards can never attain. As the chain of Prophethood is over and no one can be a companion without the company of a Prophet, their rank is unique. They spent their lives in the period which the Holy Prophet declared to be "The Best", saying: "The best people among you are the ones who belong to my lifetime period, then those who would come afterwards, then those who would come afterwards." Allah Almighty declared His pleasure with all of them, saying: "And leading everyone, the first are the Muhajirs and the Ansar, and those who followed them with virtue — Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him... this is the greatest success." (Surah At-Tauba: 100). They are the highest-ranking people in the world after the Prophets. They passed on to us the Holy Qur'an, the Sunnah and the entire Deen, and Islam reached every corner of the world due to the efforts of their sacrifice. Hence to have devout love and reverence for all the companions is the requisite of faith, and the slightest disrespect or blasphemy of any companion is a great sin; the Holy Prophet said: "Do not insult my Companions, for if anyone of you spends gold equal to Mount Uhud (in Allah's cause), it will not be equal to a Mudd, or even half a Mudd, spent by one of them." (Bukhari: 3673 / Muslim: 222). Therefore it is obligatory upon all Muslims to love and revere all the companions of the Holy Prophet.
questions.explanation: Based on the section "Excellence of Companions" in the lesson, citing Surah At-Tauba (100) and Bukhari/Muslim hadith on not insulting the companions.

questions.question: Explain the greatness of companions.
questions.answer: The greatness of the companions (Sahaba) is established both by the Qur'an and by the Ahadith of the Holy Prophet (PBUH). The Holy Prophet said: "Glad tidings for the one who saw me and for the one as well who saw the person who has seen me" — thereby giving glad tidings to the companions (Sahaba) and their successors (Tabi'in). He also said: "The best people among you are the ones who belong to my lifetime period, then those who would come afterwards, then those who would come afterwards." Almighty Allah declared His pleasure with all of them in the Holy Qur'an: "And leading everyone, the first are the Muhajirs and the Ansar, and those who followed them with virtue — Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him, and He has kept ready for them Gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide in it forever and ever; this is the greatest success." (Surah At-Tauba: 100). These auspicious personalities who attained the status of Sahaba are the highest-ranking people in the world after the Prophets. They spent their lives in the era declared "The Best" by the Prophet and they transmitted to us the Holy Qur'an, the Sunnah and the entire Deen, so that Islam reached every corner of the world through their sacrifice. Therefore, it is obligatory upon all Muslims to love and revere all the companions, and disrespecting any of them is a great sin.
questions.explanation: Drawn from the section "Greatness of Companions (Sahaba)" and "Excellence of Companions", quoting the Prophet's hadith and Surah At-Tauba (100).

questions.question: Describe the literal and terminological meaning of Sahabi (Companion).
questions.answer: The word "Sahabi" is derived from an Arabic word "Suhb", which is meant for "companionship". In Islamic terminology, a Sahabi (or companion) is someone who met with the Holy Prophet (PBUH) in the state of faith and passed away with faith.
questions.explanation: Definition given directly in the opening section of the lesson on the greatness of companions.

questions.question: What is the literal meaning of 'Ashra Mubasharah'?
questions.answer: In Arabic, "Ashra" stands for ten, and "Mubasharah" is derived from the word "Bisharah", which means "the one who is given good news". Thus, "Ashra Mubasharah" literally means the ten companions whom the Holy Prophet (PBUH) gave the glad tidings of Paradise.
questions.explanation: Explained in the lesson section "The Ten Blessed Companions".

questions.question: Outline the names of the Ten Blessed Companions.
questions.answer: The ten blessed companions (Ashra Mubasharah), whom the Holy Prophet gave the glad tidings of Paradise, are: (1) Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddique, (2) Hazrat Umar Farooq bin Khattab, (3) Hazrat Uthman bin Affan, (4) Hazrat Ali Murtaza bin Abi Talib, (5) Hazrat Talha bin Ubaidullah, (6) Hazrat Zubair bin Awam, (7) Hazrat Abdul Rehman bin Auf, (8) Hazrat Saad bin Abi Waqas, (9) Hazrat Saeed bin Zaid, and (10) Hazrat Abu Ubaidah bin Jarrah (may Allah be pleased with them all).
questions.explanation: Names given in the Hadith narrated by Hazrat Abdul Rehman bin Auf and the ten brief sketches in the lesson.

questions.answer: The Ten Companions who are given glad tidings.
